8 RAG SLOs: Recall, MRR, Freshness, Latency - Balanced
A practical scorecard to build trustworthy, fast, and affordable RAG systems - without gaming the metric.
The 8 SLOs that matter for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: recall, MRR, freshness, latency, cost, groundedness, coverage, and drift. Practical, testable, and balanced.
RAG is brilliant - until it isn’t. You tweak embeddings, widen K, add re-ranking… and somehow answers get slower, older, and still miss the mark. The fix? Treat RAG like production search: set SLOs, measure continuously, and refuse to “optimize” one metric at the expense of the product.
Let’s get you a scorecard that keeps you honest.
Why SLOs for RAG feel different
Search teams have lived with precision/recall for decades. LLM teams obsess over hallucinations and token costs. RAG sits awkwardly in the middle. Tuning it is a negotiation among quality, speed, freshness, and cost. If you track only one, you’ll break the other three. The goal here is a balanced set: enough to prevent regressions, not so many you drown in dashboards.
Below are the eight SLOs I’ve seen work in real systems, plus how to measure them without turning your team into amateur statisticians.
The 8 SLOs that matter
1) Retrieval Recall@K (must-have)
What it means: Of the ground-truth passages that contain the answer, how many show up in your top K? Why it matters: No recall, no chance. If the right text never surfaces, the LLM can’t ground itself.
SLO example: Recall@20 ≥ 0.85 on weekly eval set of 1,000 queries.
Gotchas: High K boosts recall but drags latency and cost; pair this with a latency SLO (below).
2) MRR / NDCG (rank quality, not just presence)
What it means: MRR rewards finding the correct passage early; NDCG rewards good overall ranking. Why it matters: You don’t just want the right doc - you want it early so rerankers and the LLM get better context.
SLO example: MRR@20 ≥ 0.60 on head + long-tail mixes.
Gotchas: Don’t overfit to the head queries; include “weird” real user questions in the eval set.
3) Groundedness / Hallucination Rate
What it means: Answers must cite supporting chunks, and those chunks must actually contain the facts used. Why it matters: Users forgive “I don’t know.” They don’t forgive confident nonsense.
SLO example: ≥ 95% answers have at least one valid citation; hallucination rate ≤ 2%.
How to measure: Spot-check with human raters weekly plus an automated regex/FAQ match for claims.
4) Freshness / Staleness Budget
What it means: How up-to-date are your citations? Why it matters: For product docs, pricing, or policies, last quarter’s truth can be today’s liability.
SLO example: 90th percentile citation age ≤ 7 days for dynamic corpora; ≤ 30 days for static.
Levers: Streaming ingestion, CDC to index, incremental embeddings, and time-decay in re-ranking.
5) End-to-End Latency (p50/p95/p99)
What it means: Time from user query to first token of grounded answer. Why it matters: Perceived intelligence is speed. Let’s be real: 7s feels broken.
SLO example: p50 ≤ 800ms, p95 ≤ 2.5s, p99 ≤ 4s. (Adjust for network and model size.)
Tech moves: Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vectors), approximate ANN, tight filters, fast reranker, and prompt templates sized to the task.
6) Cost per Answer (and per Correct Answer)
What it means: Total spend to serve an answer, including embedding updates, vector scans, rerankers, and LLM tokens. Why it matters: Margins. Also, costs explode quietly with wider K and fatter prompts.
SLO example: Median cost/answer ≤ $0.012; cost per correct answer ≤ $0.02.
Tip: Track cost per correct answer - it stops teams from shipping cheap-but-wrong responses.
7) Coverage & Abstention Rate
What it means: Can the system recognize when the corpus doesn’t contain an answer and abstain gracefully? Why it matters: A polite “I don’t have that” beats a polished hallucination.
SLO example: Abstain when evidence score < threshold; false-claim rate ≤ 1%.
Mechanics: Evidence scoring on top-K support, answer consistency checks, policy gates.
8) Drift & Guardrails
What it means: Detect when embeddings, prompts, or content distribution drift so far that yesterday’s SLOs no longer hold. Why it matters: A new product line, a changed embedding model, or a prompt tweak can crater quality overnight.
SLO example: Alert if weekly MRR drops >10% while recall@K is stable (signals reranker or prompt issue).
Guardrails: Toxicity/PII filters, domain-blocks, and “do-not-answer” lists with human escalation.
How the pieces fit (described, no diagram)
A minimal RAG SLO loop looks like this:
1.
Ingestion streams documents → chunker → embedding index (plus a BM25 index).
2.
Query path fans out: BM25 and ANN recall → lightweight re-ranker → context packer → LLM.
3.
Telemetry logs queries, top-K, chosen chunks, citations, tokens, latency, and costs.
4.
Evaluator runs on a curated eval set nightly: computes recall@K, MRR, groundedness, and freshness.
5.
Scoreboard tracks SLOs, alerts on drift, and shows cost per correct answer alongside latency percentiles.
Short, honest, and automatable.
Quick metrics you can actually run
Python: recall@k and MRR from labeled evals
# inputs: eval rows of {qid, rel_doc_ids, ranked_doc_ids} def recall_at_k(rel, ranked, k=20): if not rel: return 0.0 return len(set(rel) &amp; set(ranked[:k])) / len(set(rel)) def mrr_at_k(rel, ranked, k=20): rel_set = set(rel) for i, d in enumerate(ranked[:k], start=1): if d in rel_set: return 1.0 / i return 0.0 def aggregate(rows, k=20): recalls, mrrs = [], [] for r in rows: recalls.append(recall_at_k(r["rel_doc_ids"], r["ranked_doc_ids"], k)) mrrs.append(mrr_at_k(r["rel_doc_ids"], r["ranked_doc_ids"], k)) return {"recall@k": sum(recalls)/len(recalls), "mrr@k": sum(mrrs)/len(mrrs)}
DuckDB: compute latency, cost, and freshness from Parquet logs
-- logs.parquet has: ts, qid, p50_ms, p95_ms, tokens_prompt, tokens_output, -- cost_usd, topk_ids, cited_ids, cited_max_age_days, eval_correct WITH base AS ( SELECT ts::DATE AS d, p50_ms, p95_ms, cost_usd, cited_max_age_days, eval_correct FROM 'logs.parquet' ) SELECT d, approx_quantile(p50_ms, 0.5) AS p50_ms, approx_quantile(p95_ms, 0.95) AS p95_ms, avg(cost_usd) AS avg_cost, approx_quantile(cited_max_age_days, 0.9) AS p90_freshness_days, avg(CASE WHEN eval_correct THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS correctness_rate, avg(cost_usd) / NULLIF(avg(CASE WHEN eval_correct THEN 1 ELSE 0 END),0) AS cost_per_correct FROM base GROUP BY d ORDER BY d DESC;
Why DuckDB? It lets you audit your RAG runs locally, fast, over Parquet logs. Perfect for daily SLO health checks without standing up heavy infra.
A small case study: when “better recall” made answers worse
An e-commerce Q&A bot widened K from 20 → 60 and added a cross-encoder reranker. Recall@60 jumped from 0.78 to 0.92. Victory? Not quite.
•
p95 latency climbed from 1.9s → 3.4s.
•
Cost per correct answer rose 38% (more reranker + LLM context tokens).
•
Groundedness dipped because the prompt ballooned and diluted the most relevant evidence.
The fix was a hybrid plan: BM25 for precision on short queries, ANN for semantic recall on long queries, K=32 cap, and per-query evidence thresholding to keep context lean. The result: MRR +9%, p95 2.2s, cost/correct −17%, and users noticed - in a good way.
Practical tips to keep the balance
•
Define “correct” upfront. Is it exact-match? Policy-conformant? Source-cited? Align early to avoid “but my metric says…” debates.
•
Separate offline from online. Nightly evals guard against regressions; online probes catch tail-latency and drift. You need both.
•
Track cost where it happens. Attribute dollars to each stage: retrieval, rerank, LLM. Otherwise optimizations lie to you.
•
Prefer abstention to invention. It protects trust - and your brand - while you enrich the corpus.
•
Version everything. Embeddings, prompts, ranking pipelines, and eval sets. Reproducibility isn’t optional.
Conclusion
SLOs won’t make your RAG smart. They’ll make it honest. And in a world where “sounds right” is cheap, honesty is your moat. Start with these eight: recall, MRR, groundedness, freshness, latency, cost, coverage, and drift. Wire them into your daily loop. You’ll ship faster - not because you guess less, but because you know when a change helps, hurts, or quietly taxes the business.
